newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian soymeal has edge over US in Eastern markets.
newsitem.headline: Indian soymeal has edge over US in Eastern markets.

text.p: India's soymeal is poised to take advantage of Chinese and Far Eastern export markets as supplies from the United States have eased off and freight rates from That country risen, traders said on Tuesday.
"India has a competitive edge over the U.S," said Davesh Jain, chairman of the Soybean Processors' Association of India (SOPA), based in the central Indian city of Indore.
"U.S. exporters have moved out quite a sizeable quantity and the peak is over," Jain told Reuters by telephone.

The U.S. Agriculture Department (USDA) reported sales through October 24 at 1.93 million tonnes against 996,000 a year ago. Traders say the U.S. has projected 1996/97 soymeal exports at more than 6.0 million tonnes, the bulk of which go to Europe.

Jain said Indian soymeal, with a protein content of 48 percent, matches that of the U.S. which is priced at least $10 higher. Indian soymeal is currently quoted at $300 per tonne (C&F) compared to the U.S. price of $310/315 per tonne, he said.
"Indian soymeal has a better protein content for its price," said Jain. "It also has a freight advantage and is available in smaller consignments of 10,000-12,000 tonnes preferred by importers."

Jain said U.S. supplies, shipped by large Panamax vessels in huge consignments of 50,000 tonnes, have flooded markets, but Panamax freight rates had gone up by nearly 25 percent and their sailing time of five weeks compares with two weeks taken by Indian shipments to reach their destinations.
"A lot of Chinese buyers are interested in Indian soymeal for these reasons," Jain said. "We are also looking at markets in the Philippines, South Korea and Thailand."
Jain said Brazil and Argentina, two other big soymeal exporters, had already sold their stocks and were not aggressive players in world markets.
"It's basically a competition between the U.S. and India in the region," Jain said.
Traders project Indian soymeal exports in 1996/97 (November-October) lower at 2.0 million tonnes against 2.5 million in the previous year due to a production shortfall this year.
India has already committed up to 800,000 tonnes of soymeal for export from the 1996/97 crop, they said.
Its 1996/97 soybean crop is expected to fall below 4.0 million tonnes from 4.45 million in the previous year.
Jain said late sowing and flooding of some of the crop area in the central state of Madhya Pradesh had damaged at least 10 percent of the crop in the current season.
Traders have estimated world soybean output in 1996/97 at 135 million tonnes, up from 128 million in the previous year.
"But world soymeal demand is also growing," Jain said.
"In the current situation, world soymeal prices are likely to stay steady at around $300 per tonne, against $270 at the end of July and beginning of August," he added.
